title: Legal-help evaluation: Resolved problems outrank exam accuracy
desc: Centers users and frontline providers in measuring everyday justice outcomes, offering an initial framework rather than proven access gains.

kps.k: Assess legal-help AI by its contribution to resolving everyday civil legal problems, not by legal accuracy or exam performance alone.
kps.d: Hagan’s research centres unmet needs involving housing, debt, family, employment and benefits. It argues that even accurate, hallucination-free answers can fail users or cause harm if they do not support practical problem-solving. The Stanford project hub contrasts this objective with legal-exam performance; its discussion of LegalBench does not establish access-to-justice gains. The ABA Task Force endorses developing quality standards, but that endorsement does not validate any particular rubric.

qs.q: A definition of quality anchored only on legal accuracy risks missing other key needs that a person has, and that a good Legal Q-and-A interaction can provide them with.
qs.a: Measuring What Matters: Developing Human-Centered Legal Q-and-A Quality Standards through Multi-Stakeholder Research · Academia · 2024

qs.q: Rigorous evaluation of AI tools that individuals without lawyers might use for assistance with their civil problems is important to protect the public from inaccurate and potentially harmful information and to facilitate the development of accurate and useful tools.
qs.a: Addressing the Legal Challenges of AI: Year 2 Report on the Impact of AI on the Practice of Law · Regulators & courts · 2025

kps.k: Users and frontline providers should help define quality, rather than leaving standards to expert forecasts.
kps.d: Towards Human-Centered Standards reports structured interviews, design sessions and comparisons of interface complexity. Participants expressed enthusiasm about understanding the law and gaining control and dignity, but their varied needs undermined the idea of a universal user. Hagan treats these findings as exploratory patterns and hypotheses, not evidence of improved legal outcomes or sufficient grounds for comprehensive regulation. The project hub describes related work from the same research programme, not independent confirmation.

qs.q: Rather, experts’ preferences and predictions about the public’s use of AI for legal help should be counterbalanced with data about the actual preferences and behavior of the public, especially community members who need legal help and would be in the potential audience for legal services.
qs.a: Towards Human-Centered Standards for Legal Help AI · Academia · 2024

qs.q: The study’s participants indicated a general enthusiasm and optimism around how AI can help them understand the law, protect themselves, and feel a sense of control and dignity.
qs.a: Towards Human-Centered Standards for Legal Help AI · Academia · 2024

kps.k: The empirical contribution is an initial evaluation framework, not demonstrated improvement in access to justice.
kps.d: Measuring What Matters describes three sequential studies over 18 months: user interviews and fictional eviction exercises, expert ranking of candidate criteria, and expert application of criteria to sample AI eviction answers. Quantitative rankings and qualitative discussions inform a draft rubric focused on landlord-tenant questions. The supplied material provides neither numerical performance results nor actual-case outcome evidence. The hub also describes professional ratings that generate labelled data and refine criteria; automated evaluation remains exploratory. Hagan proposes translating the rubric into concrete measures and recurring audits of both human and AI services.

qs.q: Studies to Establish Quality Benchmarks Over 18 months, the Legal Design Lab conducted 3 sequential studies to establish community-driven quality metrics for Legal Q-and-A.
qs.a: Measuring What Matters: Developing Human-Centered Legal Q-and-A Quality Standards through Multi-Stakeholder Research · Academia · 2024

qs.q: Our team gathered quantitative data about users’ and experts’ rankings of the quality of AI answers, along with qualitative discussions about what makes an answer helpful or harmful.
qs.a: Measuring What Matters: Developing Human-Centered Legal Q-and-A Quality Standards through Multi-Stakeholder Research · Academia · 2024

kps.k: The debate pits potential service expansion against harm and inequality risks, while questioning idealised comparisons with human assistance.
kps.d: Hagan reports hopes that AI could identify legal issues, direct people to assistance and support case preparation, alongside concerns about fabricated information, missed deadlines, inferior services and language or digital-access barriers. These are largely forecasts, not measured outcomes in the supplied studies. She also argues that anecdotal comparisons with idealised human services can unduly restrict innovation. The material offers no direct empirical resolution of this tension; it recommends investigating specific harms, users’ responses to warnings, and jointly designed technical, interface and policy safeguards.

qs.q: When new technology-based legal services have emerged over the past decades, legal policymakers and regulators often compare them to a mythical golden standard of expert human-provided services.
qs.a: Measuring What Matters: Developing Human-Centered Legal Q-and-A Quality Standards through Multi-Stakeholder Research · Academia · 2024

qs.q: Domain experts worry about whether this enthusiasm might come at the price of low-quality information or other harms, but this worry is not helpful without clear understandings of the possible harms, of how people are likely to interact with policy measures like warning notices or technical explanations, and of the ideal solutions that community members prefer.
qs.a: Towards Human-Centered Standards for Legal Help AI · Academia · 2024

kps.k: Professional-support pilots and shared use-case evaluations offer implementation routes, but their benefits remain qualified.
kps.d: The Stanford Lab pilots tools with legal aid and courts for eviction defence, housing conditions, reentry obligations and debt relief. These initiatives aim to augment professionals’ capacity; they do not demonstrate that direct AI self-help can replace legal assistance. Separately, proposed self-help applications cover rights information, paperwork, hearings and negotiation. The ABA Year 2 report recommends sharing evaluated use cases and cites Chen and Kim’s database of more than 100 legal-aid applications. Its efficiency figures are estimates, not demonstrated aggregate gains.

qs.q: The Legal Design Lab is working with legal aid and court groups around the country to scope, prototype, and pilot new AI tools to help legal professionals better serve more of the public.
qs.a: AI & Access to Justice Initiative — project hub (Stanford Legal Design Lab) · Academia · 2025

qs.q: includes a link to a related database that provides detailed descriptions of more than 100 AI use cases for legal aid, including ratings, recommendations, and estimates of efficiency gains resulting from use of the AI tool.
qs.a: Addressing the Legal Challenges of AI: Year 2 Report on the Impact of AI on the Practice of Law · Regulators & courts · 2025

kps.k: Affordability and discoverability are access-to-justice conditions, not secondary features of technically capable tools.
kps.d: The ABA’s August 2024 report warns that subscription costs could exclude public-interest providers. Its Year 2 report notes free or discounted access through Thomson Reuters and Everlaw but calls for wider provision and continuing engagement with developers. Neither report establishes that AI costs have already widened the justice gap. Hagan’s broader online-help agenda adds accessibility, administrative burden, technical performance and discoverability to content quality: useful assistance must also be reachable and usable.

qs.q: Subscription costs for the best and most reliable legal AI tools      pose a risk of making those tools unaffordable to and inaccessible to the access-to-justice      community.
qs.a: ABA Task Force on Law and Artificial Intelligence — Year 1 Report on the Impact of AI on the Practice of Law (August 2024) · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: Examples include Thomson Reuters’ AI for Justice Legal Aid Program and Everlaw’s “Everlaw for Good” initiative.
qs.a: Addressing the Legal Challenges of AI: Year 2 Report on the Impact of AI on the Practice of Law · Regulators & courts · 2025

kps.k: The practical governance agenda extends beyond pilots to ongoing monitoring, accountability and stewardship.
kps.d: Hagan recommends recurring quality audits and continued community participation as tools evolve. Her broader civil-justice research agenda proposes using search and social-media data to track legal needs, guide outreach and investigate online-help harms; these remain proposed methods rather than established findings. The Stanford hub also features her call for statewide stewardship, without specifying its institutional duties. Together, these recommendations frame access-to-justice AI as a continuing service-governance task rather than a one-time deployment decision.

qs.q: From this 3-study sequence, the paper presents a quality rubric that can be used as the roadmap for research protocols to systematically and regularly audit AI systems’ performance at Legal Q-and-A tasks.
qs.a: Measuring What Matters: Developing Human-Centered Legal Q-and-A Quality Standards through Multi-Stakeholder Research · Academia · 2024

qs.q: Researchers could pool legal aid groups’                Google Analytics, or use SEO trafﬁc estimators, along with Google Trends and                other intermediaries’ APIs in order to track people’s online expressions of justice                problems and legal needs longitudinally.
qs.a: Legal Tech and the Future of Civil Justice · Academia · 2023

vlens.an: The curated academia-and-research sources accept the proposition that legal-help AI should be judged by practical civil-justice outcomes and user-defined quality rather than accuracy or exam performance alone. They materially develop it through participatory, multi-stakeholder research methods; a draft rubric informed by users and frontline providers; broader criteria covering actionability, accessibility, administrative burden, technical performance and discoverability; and proposals for recurring audits, harm measurement, longitudinal needs monitoring and statewide stewardship. The sources consistently distinguish these frameworks, pilots and anticipated benefits from demonstrated access-to-justice gains. Material variation concerns scope and maturity: one paper develops landlord-tenant-focused evaluation criteria, another broadens the agenda to online-help infrastructure and monitoring, and the community study concentrates on preferences, behaviour and safeguards rather than outcome measurement. One bibliographic-only record is indeterminate. Much of the substantive material comes from Margaret Hagan and the Stanford Legal Design Lab, with the project hub summarising related work, so it should not be treated as independent confirmation or as representative of academia generally.

qs.a: Measuring What Matters: Developing Human-Centered Legal Q-and-A Quality Standards through Multi-Stakeholder Research · Academia · 2024

vlens.an: These selected regulators and professional-body reports support the proposition’s broader programme of evaluating legal-help AI against practical quality, safety and access-to-justice requirements rather than relying on technical capability alone. Their common reasons are the need to protect unrepresented people from inaccurate or harmful assistance, develop quality standards, and ensure that reliable tools are affordable to public-interest providers. There is limited internal variation: the Year 1 report primarily endorses Hagan’s initial criteria and stresses affordability, while the Year 2 report adds rigorous evaluation, widespread sharing of evaluated legal-aid use cases and continuing engagement with vendors. Neither report expressly establishes that resolved civil problems should outrank accuracy metrics or exam performance, centres user participation as clearly as the synthesis does, or provides evidence of improved legal outcomes. Their claims that high costs could widen the justice gap are prospective risks, while reported efficiency gains are estimates. This assessment concerns only the curated sources supplied and does not indicate how prevalent these views are among regulators, courts or professional bodies generally.

qs.q: Rigorous evaluation of AI tools that individuals without lawyers might use for assistance with their civil problems is important to protect the public from inaccurate and potentially harmful information and to facilitate the development of accurate and useful tools.
qs.a: Addressing the Legal Challenges of AI: Year 2 Report on the Impact of AI on the Practice of Law · Regulators & courts · 2025

elens.an: The substantive 2023–2024 sources support the proposition that legal-help AI should be evaluated by whether it helps people resolve everyday civil legal problems and avoid harmful life outcomes, not by accuracy or legal-task performance alone. Their common rationale is that technically correct answers may still be unusable or harmful, while meaningful quality depends on practical actionability and evidence from users and frontline providers. They consistently treat access-to-justice benefits as prospective rather than demonstrated: the empirical work provides exploratory user research and an initial landlord-tenant-focused rubric, while the ABA endorsement identifies a need for standards without validating the rubric or proving improved outcomes. Material variation lies mainly in emphasis. The human-centred studies prioritise participatory standard-setting and concrete safeguards; the ABA report adds affordability as a condition of equitable access; and the broader civil-justice agenda materially extends evaluation to accessibility, administrative burden, technical performance, discoverability, longitudinal needs monitoring and harm measurement. One bibliographic-only record remains indeterminate and adds no substantive evidence. Because the corpus is curated, this alignment describes these selected sources rather than the prevalence of the view across researchers, policymakers or access-to-justice organisations generally.

qs.q: The rubric is an initial contribution that helps technologists, researchers, and regulators know what to measure.
qs.a: Measuring What Matters: Developing Human-Centered Legal Q-and-A Quality Standards through Multi-Stakeholder Research · Academia · 2024

elens.an: The selected 2025 sources support the proposition that legal-help AI should be evaluated by its usefulness for everyday civil justice problems, not by legal accuracy or exam performance alone. They share an emphasis on rigorous, real-world evaluation and do not claim that access-to-justice gains have already been demonstrated. There is material variation in emphasis: the Stanford Legal Design Lab centers community participation, multi-stakeholder quality criteria, professional-support pilots and statewide stewardship, while the Year 2 report stresses evaluated use-case sharing, protection from harmful information and affordable access. The latter is somewhat more focused on implementation at scale and inequality risk, but remains aligned with the proposition. These sources therefore reinforce the proposition while treating current frameworks, pilots and estimated efficiencies as preliminary rather than proven outcomes.
